Looks like Texas might go after Saban...again. There's also talk that Dabo could replace him, and Dabo didn't say never.

As much as I like Dabo, I'd like to keep Saban.

Let's look at the facts:

  • Saban is 64 years old. Paterno was 84 when he retired, Bowden was 80, but they were both forced out. Bear Bryant was 69, but retired due to his health and the fact that he wasn't winning as much (whatever that meant). Spurrier is 70, but might not be completely done. All this points to Saban having anywhere between 5 and 15 more years of coaching left in him.

  • Since 1990, Saban has spent 1 year at Toledo, 4 years at the Browns (DC), 5 years with Michigan State, 5 years with LSU, 2 years with the Dolphins, and 9 years at Alabama.

  • He and his wife are comfortable in Tuscaloosa. He's stated that he feels respected and appreciated, which is his biggest thing. Terry is a queen there, Nick is the king. He owns a Mercedes dealership, and the boosters bought him his house. His daughter got married in Bryant-Denny, and they live in Mtn Brook now (a very prestigious town near Birmingham). He has never laid down these kinds of roots anywhere else.

  • The Texas rumors from a couple of years ago remain in the air, if not completely unsubstantiated. We know his agent (Jimmy Sexton) talked to Texas, and at least one booster made an overture. When others got involved, they made sure to tell Sexton not to run them around just to push up Alabama's new contract. At that point, Sexton went silent, suggesting that Saban never had any intention of leaving. Alabama's new contract did, however, go up. A lot.

  • Saban considers himself a rebuild specialist, and doesn't like the expectations of winning fan bases. However, it's gotten pretty easy to win at Alabama, and he knows his fans aren't the ones trumpeting the "end of a dynasty" every time we lose a game. It's now less about expectations than it is about his interest (i.e. is he bored?).

  • His favorite team ever, at least from my listening to countless press conferences and paying attention to this kind of thing, was his 2003 LSU championship team. However, his next 6 favorite teams were all at Alabama (2008, 2009, 2011, 2012, 2014, 2015). He's become a lot more emotional coaching these kids, and you can hear it in what he says about his recent teams (expecially this year's). The only concern here is that his nostalgia might indicate he's done thinking about a future at Alabama, just the past.

His history suggests that if he left Alabama, one of two things would happen:

  • He'd rebuild a team for about 5-9 years, then move on to his final job for 5-10 years and retire around age 80-85

  • He'd move immediately on to his final, retirement job, but retire earlier, say age 75-80

In either case, I don't see him moving back to the NFL. He'd only do that first, so that he could back to a college program to retire if that didn't work out (again). But if he did that, he'd obviously be skipping the UT opportunity now, and why would he ever leave Alabama now for anything less than some other football royalty? The only other "royal" job openings are USC and Miami, and he's not on either radar. Hell, the Texas job isn't even open yet.

And if he was going to leave for the Texas job, why didn't he do it a few years ago before UT hired Strong? The program was already in shambles, and Saban wasn't exactly happy in T-town (I remember, the tension was palpable). A case can be made that Texas is in worse shape than when Mack Brown was forced out (at 62), but that's debatable b/c at least Strong has injected some life back into the program (see the Oklahoma victory).

Saban's rebuild mentality (i.e. come in, scrap everything, destroy everyone's morale, and build from scratch like the Marine Corps) wouldn't work as well now at UT as it would have then, and I think Saban knows that. He's also a lot softer now than he was in 2007-09 when he was rebuilding Alabama, so you have to wonder if he even wants to do it again. He's said himself that it would be really hard for him to "start all over somewhere else." He's a grandpa, after all.

The only reason we're even entertaining the thought of Saban's departure is because of his brief history at each school he's coached, but his current situation is drastically different than those before. It's like when we overthought the QB battles. Everyone thought Jake Coker would take the starting job last year, or that Cooper Bateman would take it this year. I agreed on the former, and I was wrong. So this year, I called it - Jake Coker. Why? Because Saban is way more pragmatic (predictably so) than we think he is, and of course he's going to start the most experienced guy with real playing time under his belt. This means Bateman will start next year, unless Blake Barnett comes out swinging.

And that alone might be the reason Saban leaves: The amount of talent leaving at the end of 2015.

We'll lose most of the defense, our whole backfield, most of our O-line, our kicker (thank god), and potentially our two coordinators. Can you imagine Saban without Smart? I can't, and I think the reason Smart hasn't left yet is because 1) the right job hasn't come available, and 2) he was waiting for Saban to leave, too. If Smart takes a job elsewhere, the Saban Clock starts ticking.
Another year, another coaching carousel, another shot at Nick Saban
